graphEvents.label: OpenBot approval is an ordered kind-rule-switch policy
Skilled bots approves definitions, not actions

label: OpenBot decides whether to ask with an ordered policy, first match wins: action kinds, then rules with the strictest winning, then auto-review, then Extra vigilant.

An OpenBot approval card offers Allow once, Allow for this conversation (same bot, tool, place and account), Always allow here (saved rule) and Deny; an allow reaches only the kind of action it was given on.
The team edition adds a per-action-kind administrator setting: Members choose, Ask every time, or Members do it themselves.
OpenBot's role vocabulary is owner, admin and member, decided in one app function and enforced again on the server.
OpenBot's personal edition has nobody sign in and one fixed administrator; with no identity provider the server refuses to start unless OPENBOT_SINGLE_USER=true, and still refuses a public address.

Bot ownership and visibility are separate from conversation membership: person-made bots are owned, package bots ownerless, visibility is private (owner and admins) or public, and Team Bot publication is a separate revocable record.

Skilled bots' approval is definition-level: unattended runs execute only the BOT.md and bots/config.json bytes an operator approved, hashed under the user-level state root and written only on install, enable or manual run.

A needs-you item is the human-decision primitive: a parked run ends, leaves one item under the user-level state root, and its open/answered/expired state is derived from its fields rather than stored.
bots answer records the operator's answer, enqueues one resume request keyed by the item id and advances the generation; the answer is checked for secret literals before storage.
Run records join queue, delivery and status, live under the user-level state root, and treat awaiting-decision as a terminal exit.

Turnstone's RBAC with admin, operator and viewer roles plus allow/deny/ask tool policies is the enterprise-shaped version of an approval layer, with a cleaner three-word policy vocabulary than role tree.

The smallest small-team model is one operator identity recorded on existing acts (answer, definition approval, run record), one visibility rule per bot and one shared-versus-personal memory scope, not a role system.

direction: Copying OpenBot owner/admin/member roles into skilled bots
reason: With no sign-in or tenant the roles distinguish nothing; recording who approved what gives the same protection.

direction: Copying turnstone's full RBAC and permission-string model
reason: It exists to delegate across many users and endpoints, a problem a small team does not have.

direction: Treating bots answer as an approval system
reason: It continues a parked run after the fact; it does not gate an action before it happens.

question: What is the smallest sign-in and role model for a few people sharing one machine or host, and which parts of OpenBot's owner/admin/member split and turnstone's RBAC can be dropped?
How should shared versus per-person memory be scoped when a few people use the same bots, and what does OpenBot's memory model do that skilled bots' per-bot files do not?
